summary: Gives guidelines for designing new application protocols that work well through NATs. Many protocols break when addresses are rewritten, so designers should avoid embedding addresses and similar pitfalls. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some devices change the return address on a letter. This tells people who design programs how to write them so letters still get home.

subtitle: Advice for protocol designers on building applications that survive address translation without special help.

tldr.problem: Network Address Translators rewrite addresses and ports, so many applications that pass addressing data between hosts break or need special helper code in the NAT device.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists design pitfalls and recommendations: avoid addresses and ports in payloads, prefer a single client-opened connection, use DNS names, keep headers sufficient, and expect mappings to expire.
tldr.outcome: A protocol that follows the guidelines should need no Application Level Gateway, which makes it easier to deploy. The memo is informational and sets no standard.

today: RFC 3235 is an Informational memo from January 2002 and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets no standard, so treat it as design advice.

sections.title: Why NAT Matters to Designers
sections.content:
RFC 3235 gives recommendations to authors of new protocols about the effects to consider so that special handling is not required at NAT gateway points. Other documents already cover NAT terminology (RFC 2663), protocol issues (RFC 3022, RFC 3027) and architectural implications (RFC 2993). This one is aimed at application designers.

When a protocol cannot pass cleanly through a NAT, an Application Level Gateway (ALG) may still make it work. ALGs usually run inside small routers next to the NAT, and the RFC says they should be simple. Many of the same design issues also affect firewalls, so a protocol that needs special handling by NAT or firewall products is harder to deploy.
sections.eli5: If a helper has to rewrite your message every time it passes through a gate, things get messy. It is better to write messages that need no rewriting at all.

sections.title: Basic NAT and NAPT
sections.content:
The RFC names two common forms of Traditional NAT. With Basic NAT only the IP addresses of packets are changed, and many applications work. With Network Address Port Translation (NAPT) both the IP addresses and the source and destination ports of TCP and UDP can be changed. An application that passes only port numbers works with Basic NAT but not with NAPT.

Designers are told to aim for NAPT compatibility, because it is the most widely deployed form and likely to be common in homes and small offices, where providers often give out a single IP address. Not all applications fit the NAPT model, which assumes a client-server shape with the clients in the private realm.
sections.eli5: Basic NAT is like changing only the street number on an envelope. NAPT also changes the apartment number, so anything that mentions the old numbers inside the letter gets confused.

sections.title: Recommendations for All NATs
sections.content:
Several recommendations apply whatever kind of NAT is in use.

  • Peer-to-peer is hard. Peers must each be reachable as a server, but with NAPT many machines sit behind one address. Client-server designs are more generally workable. Some NATs can support UDP peer-to-peer, depending on whether they match incoming packets by source address as well as port.
  • Use DNS names, not IP addresses, in payloads. A private address such as 192.168.1.10 in a web page is unreachable from outside, and may even point to a different machine on the reader's own network.
  • Do not assume mappings persist from one session to the next, except for statically configured bindings. Do not assume a system knows its own public address either.
  • Check multicast support. Not all NAT devices implement multicast routing protocols.

End-to-end IPSec will not function in the presence of a NAT. The RFC suggests TLS (RFC 2246) as a transport that traverses NAT cleanly.
sections.eli5: Do not write your home address inside the letter, because it may be wrong by the time the letter arrives. Write a name that anyone can look up instead.

sections.title: Designing for NAPT
sections.content:
Because NAPT is the most common form, the RFC gives it the most detail.

  • Keep addresses and ports out of payloads. An ALG could fix them, but that assumes every NAT device is updated in time for a new protocol, which is unlikely.
  • Avoid session bundles. Independent sessions such as POP or SMTP are preferred to protocols like FTP, which passes port information on one TCP connection to build a second for the data. HTTP shows that data can travel over one connection. Aim for a single connection where possible.
  • The client should open the connections. In FTP the PASV option lets the client open the data connection (see RFC 1579), so NAPT treats it like any simple TCP connection. If bundles are unavoidable, every session should start from the same end.
  • Prefer TCP. SYN and FIN packets tell a NAT when a session starts and ends. For UDP the NAT can only guess with timeouts, so an application that sends rarely may lose its translation. Protocols other than TCP and UDP are problematic with NAPT.
  • Avoid IP fragmentation. Two hosts behind one NAPT may pick matching fragmentation identifiers, making it impossible to tell fragments apart. Limit packet size or use Path MTU Discovery, and assume NATs do not reassemble fragments.
sections.eli5: It is simplest when you start every phone call yourself and keep it to one line. Calls that need a second line opened by the other person are the ones that get lost.

sections.title: Other NAT Types and Performance
sections.content:
For plain Basic NAT, many NAPT issues disappear, but applications should still use only the IP and TCP/UDP headers and avoid addressing in the payload. The X windowing system is an example: displays are addressed by ports 6000 through 6000 + n, so an administrator can map those ports to a private host. That works for Basic NAT but allows only one station behind a NAPT to use it, so it is not recommended there.

Bi-directional NAT (with a DNS ALG, RFC 2694), Twice NAT and Multi-homed NAT have requirements that are the same as for Basic NAT, or for NAPT or Basic NAT depending on how multi-homed NAT is set up. Realm Specific IP (RSIP, RFC 3102) lets clients allocate public address and port information so their packets need not be altered, which can permit IPSec, but it assumes only two realms.

Performance also matters. An application that opens and closes many TCP connections uses more NAT resources than one that uses a single connection, and new session setup typically stays a software function even where forwarding is in hardware.
sections.eli5: Some gates are fancier than others, but the same rule holds for all of them: keep your message simple and do not make the gatekeeper do extra work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. NATs have implications for IPSec, so developers should think about their choice of security method. Transport Layer Security operates across translation boundaries, while end-to-end IPSec will prove problematic in many cases.
sections.eli5: A secret code that includes your home address on the outside will break when the address is swapped. A code that only protects the message inside keeps working.
